column1: What tradeoff do isolation levels control when several database transactions run at the same time?
column2:
Data consistency versus concurrency.
Isolation sets what one transaction can observe or change while others run. Stronger guarantees prevent more kinds of inconsistent reads, but locks or retained row versions can add overhead.
Review source

column1: Which isolation level allows reading another transaction's uncommitted changes?
column2:
READ UNCOMMITTED.
A transaction can read a value before its writer commits it. If the writer later rolls the change back, the reader used a value that never became committed data.
Review source

column1: Why can repeated READ COMMITTED queries see different committed values for the same row within one transaction?
column2:
Other transactions can commit changes between statements.
READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads, not changes between statements. For example, one SELECT can see a price of 10 and a later SELECT can see 12 after another transaction commits its update.
Review source

column1: With READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT off, what locks does an ordinary READ COMMITTED SELECT use to protect its reads?
column2:
Shared data locks.
With read committed snapshot isolation (RCSI) off, a SELECT takes shared data locks rather than using row versions. These locks protect the read and do not normally last until the transaction commits.
Review source

column1: How does REPEATABLE READ protect rows already read by a transaction?
column2:
It holds shared locks on the read data until the transaction ends.
Shared locks protect the rows already read until the transaction ends. The same row therefore cannot be changed by another transaction in that period, but new rows can still match the search condition.
Review source

column1: How does SERIALIZABLE protect an indexed search range against phantom inserts?
column2:
Key-range locks held until the transaction ends.
A key-range lock covers the index interval, including gaps between existing keys. Protecting those gaps prevents another transaction from inserting a newly matching key before the first transaction finishes.
Review source

column1: Which database option makes READ COMMITTED use row-versioned reads?
column2:
READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT.
Read committed snapshot isolation (RCSI) changes how READ COMMITTED reads data. The session still uses READ COMMITTED, but ordinary reads use committed versions instead of taking shared data locks.
Review source

column1: With READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT enabled, which point in time determines committed data visible to an ordinary READ COMMITTED SELECT?
column2:
Data as it existed at the start of that statement.
A row version is an earlier copy of a changed row. The statement can use committed versions current when it starts. A later SELECT in the same transaction gets its own view.
Review source

column1: Which isolation level provides one consistent versioned view across multiple queries in a transaction?
column2:
SNAPSHOT.
SNAPSHOT keeps a common committed view across statements, beginning at the transaction's first data access. This differs from RCSI, which gives each statement its own view. The transaction can also read its own changes.
Review source

column1: With versioned READ COMMITTED reads, what blocking can still occur if two transactions update the same row?
column2:
Writer/writer blocking.
RCSI lets readers use committed row versions instead of waiting for many pending writes. It does not allow two open transactions to overwrite the same row at the same time.
Review source

column1: Under SNAPSHOT isolation, what happens if you update a row another transaction changed and committed after your snapshot began?
column2:
An update conflict aborts the transaction.
The update conflicts with a change committed after the snapshot began. SQL Server aborts the transaction instead of overwriting that newer change. Retry the whole unit of work with a new snapshot when appropriate.
Review source

column1: With one item left, why can two READ COMMITTED transactions oversell when each reads stock and then decrements it unconditionally?
column2:
Both transactions can read the same committed stock before either updates it.
With one unit left, both transactions can read 1 before either updates the row. They can then decrement it in turn. Put the availability test in the UPDATE so only a qualifying write succeeds.
Review source

column1: After a conditional UPDATE for a unique ProductID, what tells you whether the stock reservation succeeded?
column2:
@@ROWCOUNT, checked immediately after the UPDATE.
Read @@ROWCOUNT before another statement can change it. With a unique ProductID, 1 means the reservation update succeeded. Zero means no row matched, so do not create an order based on that attempt.
Review source

column1: With optimized locking, how does lock after qualification (LAQ) evaluate a row before locking it for modification?
column2:
It tests the predicate using the latest row version committed as of statement start.
A predicate is a condition that decides whether a row qualifies. LAQ tests it against a committed version before taking a modification lock. It can skip a nonqualifying row without waiting for a writer.
Review source

column1: Which isolation level and database option let optimized locking use lock after qualification (LAQ)?
column2:
READ COMMITTED with READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT enabled.
Optimized locking does not by itself enable LAQ for every statement. LAQ requires READ COMMITTED with row versioning enabled by RCSI. Stricter isolation or conflicting locking hints can prevent its use.
Review source

column1: Under lock after qualification (LAQ), what does SQL Server do if a matching row changes before it can update it?
column2:
The engine rechecks the predicate after resolving the write conflict.
The earlier predicate result can become stale while another transaction changes the row. The engine checks the changed row again, so a row that no longer meets the condition is not updated.
Review source

column1: Why avoid waiting for user input or external API calls inside an open database transaction?
column2:
Long waits can prolong lock or row-version retention.
While the application waits, the database can still need to hold locks or preserve older versions. Shortening the open transaction reduces the time other work can be blocked and the time versions can accumulate.
Review source

column1: Which lock can block even a READ UNCOMMITTED SELECT during a schema change?
column2:
A schema-modification (Sch-M) lock.
READ UNCOMMITTED avoids shared data locks for ordinary reads, not schema-stability locks. A schema-modification lock conflicts with the schema-stability lock, so the SELECT can still wait during the change.
Review source

column1: Which concurrency model uses row versions instead of shared data locks for ordinary reads?
column2:
Optimistic concurrency.
Optimistic reads use earlier row versions instead of placing shared locks on the data for ordinary reads. This reduces reader-writer blocking, but write operations still need protection against concurrent changes.
Review source

column1: Which SQL Server table hint requests update locks for reads and holds them until the transaction ends?
column2:
UPDLOCK.
An update lock reserves the option to modify a row after reading it. UPDLOCK holds these locks until the transaction ends. If the operation takes a table-level lock, it uses an exclusive lock instead.
Review source

column1: Which isolation level does the SQL Server HOLDLOCK table hint apply?
column2:
SERIALIZABLE.
HOLDLOCK applies SERIALIZABLE behavior to the referenced table or view for the transaction. It does not set the session isolation level for every other object the transaction reads.
Review source

column1: Which table hint requests locking reads instead of row versions under READ COMMITTED with READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT enabled?
column2:
READCOMMITTEDLOCK.
The hint makes this table access use shared data locks despite the database's row-versioned READ COMMITTED configuration. It changes the referenced access, not the database-wide setting.
Review source

column1: What is the default READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT setting in Azure SQL Managed Instance?
column2:
OFF.
Azure SQL Managed Instance defaults to locking READ COMMITTED reads. Azure SQL Database defaults to versioned READ COMMITTED reads instead. Check the actual database option because administrators can change it.
Review source
